items.prompt: Which property means every access to regulated data is recorded: who, what, when?
choices: Auditability
Immutability of evidence
Retention
items.explanation: Auditability is the durable trail of who did what and when.

items.prompt: Which property says regulated data should be deleted on a schedule instead of kept forever?
choices: Auditability
Immutability of evidence
Boundedness
items.explanation: Boundedness gives data a lawful lifetime, after which it goes.

items.prompt: Which property limits data and access to only what the job needs?
choices: Boundedness
Minimality
Auditability
items.explanation: Minimality is least data to the fewest people and services.

items.prompt: Which property means the record of the past cannot be quietly edited?
choices: Immutability of evidence
Boundedness of data lifetime
Auditability
items.explanation: If the record can be rewritten it is a story, not evidence.

items.prompt: When does a regulator mostly show up?
choices: On every single request that a user sends, in the same way a normal client calls it
Only at launch
After the fact, asking the system to prove something about its past
items.explanation: Regulators ask about past behavior, usually at audits or incidents.

items.prompt: A user judges a system by what it does now. What does a regulator judge it by?
choices: How quickly it can respond to a request today, under normal load
Whether it can later prove it acted lawfully
How cheaply it runs
items.explanation: The regulator's question is about provable history, not present performance.

items.prompt: Which question does auditability answer?
choices: Who did what to this data, and when?
How long may we keep this data before deleting it?
Which fields may this service see?
items.explanation: The other two questions belong to boundedness and minimality.

items.prompt: Which is the best example of minimality?
choices: A log kept for seven years so that auditors can review it later
A job that deletes rows
A support screen that shows only the last four digits of a card
items.explanation: Showing the least data needed is minimality; the other two are auditability and boundedness.

items.prompt: An auditor asks: prove that nobody outside the billing team read customers' bank account numbers last year. Which property must the architecture already have?
choices: Auditability: a durable trail of who read that field
Boundedness: delete the field once its lawful lifetime has ended
Minimality: remove access from every service right now
Immutability: hash all the stored account numbers
items.explanation: The question is about past reads, so only a recorded trail can answer it. Minimality limits future access but does not prove the past.
items.reference:
Four things a regulator asks you to prove
🔎 auditability: who did what, when
🔒 minimality: only what is needed, only who needs it
⏳ boundedness: a lawful lifetime, then gone
🧾 immutability: the record cannot be quietly rewritten
Why: each property answers a different question about the system's past.
items.learnMore:
Four questions, four properties

Auditability records access, minimality limits it, boundedness ends the data's life, and immutability keeps the record itself honest. A system can have three and still fail the fourth.

Common mistake

Treating them as one thing called logging. A complete log with a hole in minimality or retention still fails.
items.reflection: Think of a bank vault, a hospital chart, or a school grade book. Which of the four promises does it make, and which does it quietly lack?

items.prompt: A team keeps every customer record forever because deleting feels risky. Which property is missing, and why does a regulator care?
choices: Auditability: forever-data cannot be written to any log at all
Immutability: old rows cannot be hashed
Minimality: oldest rows are the most visible to users
Boundedness: data past its lawful life is itself a liability
items.explanation: Keeping data beyond its lawful lifetime is a failure on its own, regardless of how well it is protected.

choices: Auditability: events are not being written to the log at all today
Minimality: support sees too many tables
Immutability of evidence: the record can be quietly rewritten
Boundedness: the log has no lifetime
items.explanation: Recording is not enough; evidence that its custodians can edit is only a story.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly separates minimality from auditability?
choices: Minimality records every read; auditability limits readers
Minimality limits who may read; auditability records who did read
Minimality is about how long data lives, while auditability is about how much data there is
Both only matter once a breach has happened
items.explanation: One is a control on access, the other is a record of access. A system needs both.

items.prompt: Why can't a retrofitted audit trail answer questions about last year?
choices: Auditors only accept logs that were created after the audit date was announced
The overwritten history is already gone
Logs cannot be added
items.explanation: A trail only remembers from the day it starts.

items.prompt: From when does a newly added audit trail remember?
choices: From the day it ships
From the system's first day
From last year's audit
items.explanation: It cannot see backwards.

items.prompt: When rows are updated in place, what happens to the old value?
choices: It is kept in a hidden column that nobody normally looks at
It is archived
It is lost when the new value lands
items.explanation: An in-place update replaces the value; no history is kept unless designed in.

items.prompt: These four properties are called structural because they depend on...
choices: Which button an admin clicks
How data flows and is stored
The color of the dashboard
items.explanation: They are properties of the design, not a feature toggle.

items.prompt: When is it cheaper to decide how access is recorded?
choices: At design time
After five services depend on the raw table
They cost the same
items.explanation: Retrofits must untangle existing assumptions.

items.prompt: Logs are deleted after 30 days. What can the team say about month six?
choices: Everything, from the database
Only who wrote, not who read
Nothing, the evidence is gone
items.explanation: Rotated-out logs cannot be recovered.

items.prompt: Paperwork written after launch can describe a system, but cannot...
choices: Explain to a new engineer how the system works in general
Create evidence that was never recorded
List services
items.explanation: Documents describe; only recorded events prove.

items.prompt: Retrofitting field-level access mainly means...
choices: Untangling services that already assume full access
Writing one new if-statement and then deploying it quickly to production
Buying a database
items.explanation: The work is in the existing consumers, not the new check.

items.prompt: Larch Pay ships an audit trail today. An auditor asks who read a record eight months ago. What can the team show?
choices: Everything, because the trail also covers all earlier data
Nothing for that period; the trail starts today
Reads, but not writes, from the old system
A reconstruction built from the new trail's format
items.explanation: A trail records from its start. Earlier history needs evidence that was already being kept.
items.reference:
What a retrofit cannot recover
🗓️ history before the retrofit is gone
📝 rows already overwritten stay overwritten
🕸️ services that read raw tables must be untangled
➡️ trail starts the day it ships
Why: evidence can only be kept going forward; it cannot be created for the past.
items.learnMore:
Evidence has a start date

A new audit trail answers questions about the future. Questions about before it existed have no answer, no matter how well the trail is built.

Common mistake

Planning to start recording when an audit is announced. The audit asks about the period before the announcement.
items.reflection: Think of keeping receipts, a medical history, or a photo record of a home before a move. What do you wish you had started recording earlier?

items.prompt: Which retrofit is hardest?
choices: Adding field-level gating when five services already read the raw table
Adding a new log table that records events only from the day it is created, going forward
Adding a retention field to new records
Adding a column storing the writer's name
items.explanation: Gating changes behavior that others depend on; the others only add new data.

The audit should have been scheduled sooner

items.explanation: The failure was structural: nothing was designed to remember.

items.prompt: What does a last_modified_by column remember?
choices: Every change ever made to the row, in order
Every read
Only the most recent change
items.explanation: A single column holds one value.

items.prompt: In an append-only log, how is a mistake fixed?
choices: By editing the old event in place and saving it
By appending a new correcting event
By deleting
items.explanation: The original stays exactly as written.

items.prompt: Current state in this design is...
choices: Built from the log by reading forward
The log itself, stored in a second copy
A copy kept offline
items.explanation: The log is the memory; state is derived.

items.prompt: Does the audit log replace the operational database?
choices: Yes, it takes over every job the database has had until now
Only for reads
No, it sits beside it as memory of the past
items.explanation: The database still serves requests.

items.prompt: What can an append-only log do to an old event?
choices: Overwrite it when the actor is an administrator
Nothing, it only adds new ones
Reorder it
items.explanation: Immutability of past events is the whole idea.

items.prompt: An audit event records the actor, the field, the action and...
choices: A timestamp
The full password
The service's source code
items.explanation: When it happened is part of the proof.

items.prompt: Which structure can answer "who touched this over twelve months"?
choices: A latest-value column
A cache
A full history log
items.explanation: Only full history answers a question about a period.

items.prompt: Why does each event get a sequence number?
choices: To compress the event so that it takes less disk space
To give it a fixed place in the order
To encrypt it
items.explanation: Order matters when reconstructing what happened.

items.prompt: Support staff may edit the free-text reason on audit events. Why does this break the log?
choices: Text fields cannot be stored in an append-only log at all
Editing makes the log slower to search
Nobody can tell a clarification from a cover-up
Reasons are only valid for write events
items.explanation: Once any written field is editable, the log is no longer a record of the past.
items.reference:
Overwrite vs append
✏️ column: keeps only the latest change
📚 append-only log: keeps every event
🩹 a correction is a new event
🧱 current state is built from the log
Why: history survives only if nothing is ever edited in place.
items.learnMore:
A column forgets, a log remembers

A last_modified_by column answers who touched it last. The auditor asked for twelve months, which only a full sequence of events can give.

Common mistake

Letting an event be edited "just to fix a typo". The fix must be a new event that points to the old one.
items.reflection: Think of a paper ledger kept in pen, where mistakes are crossed out and rewritten on the next line. Why does that make it more trustworthy than erasing?

items.prompt: A typo is found in event 4821. Which handling keeps the log trustworthy?
choices: Edit event 4821 and mention the change in a separate ticket
Append a new event stating the correction and who made it
Delete 4821 and append a fixed copy
Overwrite 4821 only if the editor is an admin
items.explanation: Correct by adding; the original must remain visible.

items.prompt: Which class would a tax ID get?
choices: PII_RESTRICTED
INTERNAL, with logging switched on
PUBLIC
items.explanation: Tax IDs are the most sensitive class.

items.prompt: Which class would a display name get?
choices: PII_RESTRICTED
INTERNAL
PUBLIC
items.explanation: A display name is meant to be shown.

items.prompt: A wiki saying "be careful with PII" is...
choices: A strong control, since everyone has read it carefully by now
Not a control, since nothing checks it at request time
Required by databases
items.explanation: Controls are consulted when the request happens.

items.prompt: Where is minimality enforced?
choices: In code, at request time
In a wiki page that every engineer is asked to read
In a meeting
items.explanation: Only code can check every request.

items.prompt: A new service asks for the customer table with no field list. What is the default?
choices: All fields, then revoke later
Only PII
PUBLIC fields only
items.explanation: The default posture is exclusion.

items.prompt: Does the gate log an access when it redacts a field?
choices: No, only allowed reads
Yes, allowed or not
Only for admins
items.explanation: A denied attempt is still worth recording.

items.prompt: What does the gate return for a field outside the caller's scope?
choices: A redacted value
The real value
An empty database
items.explanation: The caller still gets the record, minus the field.

items.prompt: Who gets PII_RESTRICTED fields by default?
choices: Any authenticated service inside the company network
All staff
Named services only, every access logged
items.explanation: Restricted means named and logged.

items.prompt: An analytics service asks for the customer table to build dashboards, with no field list. What should the gate do?
choices: Return INTERNAL fields as well, since the analytics team works inside the company
Return everything and revoke if someone objects
Return nothing
Return PUBLIC fields only until specific extra fields are named and reviewed
items.explanation: Exclusion is the default; a stated, reviewed need widens it.
items.reference:
Classify, then gate
🟢 PUBLIC: any authenticated service
🟡 INTERNAL: documented business need
🔴 PII_RESTRICTED: named services, every access logged
🚪 gate checks scope at request time, logs allowed or not
Why: a rule that nothing consults at request time is a hope, not a control.
items.learnMore:
Controls run at request time

A policy page is evidence of intent. A gate that compares caller scope with field class on every request is the control. Redaction plus a logged attempt gives both safety and a signal.

Common mistake

Granting broad access first and planning to revoke later. Revocation after the fact leaves an untracked exposure window.
items.reflection: Think of a building with keycards. What is the difference between a sign saying staff only and a door that checks your card?

items.prompt: The gate redacts a restricted field for svc-analytics. Is logging that attempt still worth it?
choices: No, nothing was disclosed so nothing happened that anyone needs to review
Only if the service is external
Yes, repeated denied requests are an early warning signal
Only once per day per service
items.explanation: Attempts reveal intent; logging only successes hides that pattern.

items.prompt: Each service with access to restricted fields has the same independent 4% yearly chance of compromise and can query 50,000 records. Going from 3 services to 6, how does expected exposure change?

It stays at 6,000 since the per-service odds are unchanged by the count
It quadruples, from 6,000 to 24,000
It rises by 4%, to about 6,240
items.explanation: Expected exposure is services x records x odds, so doubling the services doubles it. The odds are an assumption.

items.prompt: Boundedness answers which question?
choices: Who is allowed to read this data inside the company?
How long should this data exist?
Who read it?
items.explanation: Boundedness is about lifetime.

items.prompt: A retention period attaches to the data's...
choices: Classification
Size
Author of the first record
items.explanation: Different classes have different lawful lifetimes.

items.prompt: How often does the retention scheduler run?
choices: Only when someone on the team remembers to run it
Once at launch
On a fixed cycle such as daily
items.explanation: Enforcement needs a regular schedule.

items.prompt: When the scheduler deletes a record, is the deletion logged?
choices: No, because deletion erases all evidence of the record
Yes, deletion is an auditable event
Only if it fails
items.explanation: The log is how deletion is proven.

items.prompt: Why is "we will clean up eventually" not boundedness?
choices: No process enforces a deadline
Cleaning up old data is not permitted by regulators
Eventually is too fast
items.explanation: Boundedness needs an enforced deadline.

items.prompt: A record has a 24-month period and is 10 months old. What does the scheduler do?
choices: Deletes it
Anonymizes it now
Leaves it alone
items.explanation: It is not past its deadline.

items.prompt: When is the retention period assigned?
choices: At audit time
At write time
At deletion time
items.explanation: The record must carry its lifetime from the start.

items.prompt: Deleting regulated data is...
choices: Itself an event a regulator may ask about
Exempt from auditability, since the data no longer exists
Never allowed
items.explanation: Deletion belongs in the trail.

items.prompt: A team keeps all data forever because deleting is scary. What is the architectural gap?
choices: No classified retention period and no process that enforces it
The audit log is missing a column for deletion reasons and codes
The database is too small
Records are not hash-chained
items.explanation: Boundedness needs both a period attached to the data and a job that applies it.
items.reference:
Retention as a process
🏷️ retention attached to the classification
📅 a scheduler runs on a fixed cycle
🗑️ deletion or anonymization at the deadline
🧾 the deletion itself is logged
Why: a deadline nobody enforces is not a deadline.
items.learnMore:
Deletion is also evidence

The deletion event is the only proof a record was removed on time. Without it the claim is an assertion.

Common mistake

Deleting quietly. The record is gone and so is any proof that it was deleted correctly.
items.reflection: Think of a library with a return date, or a subscription with an end date. Who or what actually enforces it?

choices: The scheduler ran too often
Deleted rows should have been archived
The auditor should check the database
The deletion itself left no evidence
items.explanation: With no event, "we deleted it" is only an assertion.

Delete it without logging
Delete or anonymize it and append a deletion event
Flag it for manual review in 30 days
items.explanation: Past deadline and not held means act and record the action.

items.prompt: In a hash chain, each event's hash covers its content plus...
choices: The next event's hash after it
A random number
The previous event's hash
items.explanation: Linking to the previous hash is what chains them.

items.prompt: What does the chain let you do about tampering?
choices: Prevent it
Detect it
Hide it
items.explanation: It is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof.

items.prompt: What does verification do?
choices: Recomputes every hash from the start and compares
Checks only the last hash that was stored in the log
Deletes bad events
items.explanation: Comparison with stored values exposes mismatches.

items.prompt: If event 5 is edited, which later hashes become inconsistent?
choices: Only event 5
None
All of them
items.explanation: Each later hash was built on the one before.

items.prompt: What does the first failing position tell investigators?
choices: Who the person was that made the change
Where the earliest tampering is
How many read it
items.explanation: It gives a place to start.

items.prompt: What is the first event's previous hash?
choices: A fixed start value
The last event's hash
A random value
items.explanation: The chain needs a defined beginning.

items.prompt: Does the chain stop a database admin from editing a row?
choices: Yes, it blocks every write to the stored rows
Only at night
No, it makes the edit detectable
items.explanation: Prevention needs access control.

items.prompt: When should verification be run?
choices: Never, since the chain is tamper-proof once written
On a schedule and before an audit response
Only after a breach is announced
items.explanation: Regular checks shorten the window of undetected edits.

items.prompt: Event 4821 of 9000 is edited. What does verification report?
choices: Only 4821 as bad, with every event after it still shown as valid
4821 as the first failure, with later events also inconsistent
All 9000 events as bad with no starting point
Nothing, because the edit was in the middle

items.prompt: What is a legal hold?
choices: An order to keep data past its normal deadline
A request to delete data sooner than the normal deadline allows
A password
items.explanation: Holds override normal retention.

items.prompt: While a hold is active, should expired data be deleted?
choices: Yes, on the normal schedule regardless of orders
Only half
No, it must be kept
items.explanation: Deleting held data can itself be a violation.

items.prompt: Is a held-back record logged?
choices: No, because nothing happened to the record at all
Yes, with a note that deletion was skipped
Only if edited
items.explanation: The skip is a decision worth recording.

items.prompt: When must the hold be checked?
choices: Before deletion
After deletion has been completed and confirmed
Never
items.explanation: Deleted data cannot be restored.

items.prompt: Can a log restore data deleted before a hold arrived?
choices: Yes, always
Only for PUBLIC data
No
items.explanation: A log records events, not content.

items.prompt: A hold lifts on a record already past deadline. What does the next run do?
choices: Keeps it forever
Deletes it
Asks the auditor
items.explanation: It is now past deadline and not held.

items.prompt: Two regulations disagree on retention. Who decides?
choices: A person, informed by legal advice
The scheduler, using whichever deadline it finds first
The shorter
items.explanation: Conflicts need judgment.

items.prompt: Why log a held-back record?
choices: To make the log longer and harder to read quickly
To delete
To show the skip was deliberate
items.explanation: It separates a lawful hold from an oversight.

items.prompt: Why must the retention job log a record it skipped because of a hold?
choices: So the record is deleted at the next run without anyone checking
So the hold is lifted automatically
So the team can prove the skip was a deliberate, lawful decision
So the log stays small
items.explanation: Without the event, a hold and an oversight look identical later.
items.reference:
Retention meets a legal hold
📅 past deadline, no hold: delete and log
⚖️ past deadline, hold: keep and log the skip
🕐 not past deadline: untouched
🔍 check the hold before deleting, never after
Why: a skipped deletion needs a record just as a deletion does.
items.learnMore:
Three outcomes, not two

The job's choice is delete, keep because of a hold, or leave alone. Logging the held case lets a team show later that keeping the data was lawful and deliberate.

Common mistake

Logging only deletions. Then an auditor cannot tell a lawful hold from an oversight.
items.reflection: Think of a court order to preserve documents, or a recall notice on a product. What routine process must it override, and how would you prove it did?
